_readme: Searches for a consular list that were carried out and found nothing usable. This file exists so the next pass does not repeat them. A gap is as much a result as a source: the standing rule is to check every sending country for every city, and without this the same fruitless search gets run again every few months. Each entry says what was looked for, where, what was actually found, and what would change the answer.

gaps.found: WRONG WHEN FIRST WRITTEN, corrected the same day. All four lists are live and read cleanly: the London embassy district doctor list gives 37 entries with parse_diplo_table_list, all 37 carrying their own languages, and the Edinburgh consulate lawyer list gives 7, all with languages.
gaps.why: The original entry here said not one of the 44 entries was in a city we cover, because the check asked for cities whose country is "United Kingdom" and the site files London, Manchester and Edinburgh under "UK" instead. All three ARE cities on the site. The lists were ingested once that was understood.
gaps.wouldChange: Nothing: this is no longer a gap. It is kept as a record of the mistake, because the same query would make it again. Two spellings of one country is a live defect in cities-data.js.

gaps.found: One list, Stand 09.07.2024, sectioned by city: Auckland, Wellington, Blenheim, Christchurch, Dunedin. Four of those five are cities we cover.
gaps.why: The page states that the correspondence language is English unless an entry says otherwise: "Korrespondenzsprache ist - sofern nicht anders angegeben - Englisch." So a German claim exists only where an entry spells one out, and only two do: Glaister Ennor in Auckland ("Sprachen: Englisch, Deutsch, Franzoesisch") and Hesketh Henry in Auckland ("Herr Bachmann spricht Deutsch"). Neither survived reading: the block reader takes the city heading as the name for both. English is the local language in New Zealand, so the rest of the list says nothing this directory can use.
gaps.wouldChange: A reader for this page's two-column table shape would recover two Auckland firms. Two rows is not worth a reader on its own, but the same shape may turn up elsewhere on wellington.diplo.de and the neighbouring missions.

gaps.found: The service A-Z has entries for Anwaelte and Uebersetzer and none for Aerzte.
gaps.why: Germany publishes no doctor list for Australia, and its translator page publishes no list of its own: it points at NAATI and AUSIT instead. The lawyer list was read and is in the directory.
gaps.wouldChange: NAATI is the Australian accreditation body for translators and interpreters and publishes a searchable register by language. That is an official, language-defined register and is the obvious next source for Australian translators.

gaps.found: The register exists and is exactly the right shape: Australia's only official directory of certified translators and interpreters, searchable by language.
gaps.why: It is not open data. The search is a Gravity Forms POST behind an AJAX nonce and a reCAPTCHA, and practitioners opt in to appear. Working around a reCAPTCHA is defeating an access control the operator put there on purpose, so this is not a source to scrape. Reading it is a matter of asking NAATI, not of writing a reader.
gaps.wouldChange: A data request or a licence from NAATI. AUSIT, the practitioners' association, runs its own directory and has not been checked yet.

gaps.found: Four lists behind an explicit roster claim, "you will find below the lists of professionals (who also speak Italian)": doctors, lawyers, notaries, translators. The doctors and the lawyers are both in the directory now.
gaps.why: The lawyers list was held back on the first pass because no reader could see its two columns; scripts/parse_pdf_columns.cjs was written for that shape and reads it, and three of its eleven Sydney-addressed entries are published. The other two lists are still out. The translators print a mobile and an email per entry and no address at all, so no row can be placed in a city, and the stated scope is NSW rather than Sydney. The notaries are a two-column layout whose cut falls inside the text, which parse_pdf_columns detects and refuses rather than publishing four surnames glued to one address.
gaps.wouldChange: For the notaries, a reader that can follow columns that do not line up. For the translators, an address from somewhere else entirely: the consulate does not print one.

gaps.found: A roster list of sworn translators working into and out of German, fourteen of whose entries a reader can see, filed in the registry under Santiago.
gaps.why: The list covers the whole of Chile and writes its addresses as "<street> <number>, <town>" with no postcode, which is a shape localityOf does not recognise, so every row falls back to the city the manifest names. Seven of the fourteen are in comunas of Santiago (Providencia, Nunoa, Las Condes, Vitacura, Recoleta) and belong there. The rest are in Vina del Mar, Curico, Los Angeles, Temuco and San Pedro de la Paz, between 100 and 670 km away, and would have gone out as Santiago providers. Telling a comuna of Santiago from a town in the south needs a list of comunas that we do not hold, so the whole source waits rather than half of it going out wrong.
gaps.wouldChange: Not what this entry said on 2026-08-23, which was to teach localityOf to read a town after the last comma where there is no postcode. That was tried and measured on 2026-08-23 and it is wrong: outside Europe the last piece of an address is a district far more often than a town. It read Silom as a town rather than Bangkok, Tay Ho rather than Hanoi, El Poblado rather than Medellin, Vake rather than Tbilisi, and it read "Tepic 139, Roma Sur" in Mexico City as Rome. 320 published rows would have been refused as being in the wrong city, 9 of them rows this ingest wrote. There is no way to tell a district from a town by shape, only by gazetteer. So what would change the answer is a list of place names that says which is which, for Chile a list of the comunas of Greater Santiago, and nothing short of that. Until then this source stays out.

gaps.found: The page exists and was read. It is headed "Vertrauensarzt und Vertrauensanwalt" and gives the embassy's trusted law firm (UEPA advokati, Prague 8) plus two more (PRK Partners, Roedl & Partner) with street addresses, and three hospitals that treat foreign patients. Real providers, real addresses, last updated 24.01.2025.
gaps.why:
It makes no claim about language, which is the only thing this directory indexes. The page says the embassy gives no legal advice and that these firms may be contacted, "alle Angaben sind unverbindlich und ohne Gewaehr". It never says the lawyers work in German, French or Italian, and the German wording is the German edition of a site that also has French and Italian editions rather than a statement about the firms. It closes by pointing readers at the German, French or Italian embassy websites for more, which is a source telling us it is not the one making the claim. Publishing these as German-speaking lawyers would be inventing the finding.

The 403 that blocked the first attempt is solved and worth recording: eda.admin.ch refuses a plain fetch, curl with a browser user agent, and Apify's RAG browser alike, but apify/website-content-crawler with crawlerType playwright:firefox through the RESIDENTIAL proxy group with apifyProxyCountry CH returns 200. That route is free and works for any WAF like it.
gaps.wouldChange: A Swiss page for some country that does state a working language. The Czech one is the shape the FDFA uses and it does not, so the seam is probably dead for this directory whatever the country. Check one more of a different shape before spending anything on it, and note that the German and English editions of several country pages return the site-wide navigation or a 404 rather than a list, so the country and the edition both have to be right.

gaps.found: A per-country list of interpreters and translators compiled by the Dutch embassy, with an explicit per-entry language pair on every row ("Vertaler (Nederlands-Portugees-Nederlands)"), which is the strongest kind of claim there is. Fetches cleanly with a browser user agent.
gaps.why: The entries carry a telephone, a mobile and an e-mail and NO address, so no row can be placed in a city and the address gate refuses all of them. The same shape as the Italian consulate translator list for Sydney. Country slugs are Dutch and do not follow the English name: /tolken-vertalers/spanje is a 404, so each country has to be found rather than guessed.
gaps.wouldChange: A way to place a provider that publishes no address. Everything else about these lists is ideal, and the lawyer lists (/advocaten-<country>) may carry offices where the translator lists do not; only Thailand has been read.

gaps.found: Nothing. The Dublin post publishes passports, civil status, nationality, legalisation and notarial competence, and no list of lawyers, doctors or translators.
gaps.why: Belgium has a country site per post on a clean subdomain, but what each post publishes is up to the post. Four of them carry lists and are already read (Portugal, Hungary, South Africa, Thailand); the paths differ between them, so there is no pattern to enumerate. Dublin was tried because it would have been the first list for a city that holds one provider.
gaps.wouldChange: Nothing systematic. Belgian posts have to be checked one at a time, at a low hit rate.

gaps.found: The best-shaped source found in weeks, and it cannot be used. "Forteckning over advokater/Rechtsanwalte i Tyskland", March 2026, 43 lawyers under city headings BERLIN, DUSSELDORF, FRANKFURT, HAMBURG, HANNOVER, KARLSRUHE, KASSEL, MUNCHEN, ROSTOCK and STUTTGART, six of which are our cities. The page states the roster claim, "en lista over de svensk- och engelsktalande advokater i Tyskland som ambassaden har kannedom om", and on top of that every single entry carries its own languages in brackets: "(svenska, engelska)", "(engelska)", "(svenska, engelska, finska, franska)". Per-entry claims are the strongest evidence this directory can hold, and it would add Swedish, which we have almost none of.
gaps.why:
No extraction of the PDF preserves which address belongs to which lawyer, and the addresses are the one thing a row cannot go out without.

It is set as three columns, NAMN | ADRESS | TEL/FAX/EPOST/WEBBPLATS, and the columns are aligned by order rather than by line: the first address block starts two lines above the name it belongs to. Zipping the two streams looked possible and the first five pair correctly, then they drift, because neither column can be segmented reliably. Column text bleeds across the gutters often enough that there is no run of positions blank on even 97% of lines, so a page has to be cut at a fixed offset, which slices words in half; and the header that gives the offsets appears on page 1 of 5 only.

Reading it linearly instead is worse in a way that is easy to miss. It looks perfect, one complete entry after another, and it is not: one block came out holding Jurgen Busch, Nils Gruske and Truls Hebrant with a single postcode, 12205 Berlin, which is Hebrant's. Busch is at Kurfurstendamm 29 in 10719 and Gruske at Mauerstr. 83-84 in 10117. Publishing that block would have put two lawyers at a third one's office under an official-list badge.

Both readers were written, measured and thrown away. Nothing was published from this source.
gaps.wouldChange:
A reader that works from the PDF's text positions rather than from extracted lines, so a name and an address can be matched by the vertical band they share. pdftotext IS on the PATH here (/mingw64/bin/pdftotext), which scripts/pdf_text.cjs says it is not, so `pdftotext -bbox` is available and gives coordinates per word. That is the tool for this and for any other consular list set in columns, of which there are several already held back.

Worth building, because there are 19 more Swedish lists behind this one. They are not guessable by URL: the paths differ per post (advokatlista, advokatlistan, advokater-i-<country>, faq-.../advokat). Take them from https://www.swedenabroad.se/sv/sitemap.xml and grep for advokat, which is how these 20 were found. Relevant to our cities: Greece, India, China, Mexico, Austria, Spain (Madrid), Thailand, Germany, USA (New York), Cambodia, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Slovakia, Slovenia.

gaps.country: Cambodia, India, Nepal (and the rest of the Swedish set)
gaps.found: Six more Swedish lists downloaded and read. Three carry per-entry language claims and are worth having. Cambodia is the cleanest of any source seen: a literal "Languages: English, French, Chinese & Khmer" line on each firm, plus Address, Telephone, Email and Services, over Phnom Penh. India annotates each firm in prose, "The firm has English and Hindi speaking staff", "The staff also speak Punjabi, Tamil, Bengali and also some foreign languages like German", across many Indian cities. Nepal does the same for Kathmandu, "Staffs and lawyers in fluent to speak and communicating in English, Nepali and Hindi". All three cover cities that hold one or two rows now.
gaps.why:
They need a reader nobody has written. Cambodia and India are two independent stacks of labelled blocks side by side, not a table: each firm gives its own labelled fields, and the two columns have nothing to do with each other line by line. parse_pdf_table_columns.cjs assumes the first column holds names and the second holds their addresses, so it paired the left column's firms with the right column's addresses and produced five wrong rows. It refuses that shape now rather than guessing: a field label in the first column is what gives a block layout away. parse_labelled_blocks.cjs understands the labels but not the columns, and ran one firm's languages into the next firm's name.

China (Beijing and Shanghai) and Sri Lanka were read and hold no language claim at all, so those three are out for good rather than waiting on a reader.
gaps.wouldChange: Splitting the page into columns first, which parse_pdf_table_columns.cjs already does well by clustering cell start offsets, and then running a labelled-block parse down each column independently instead of pairing them across. That is one reader combining two that already exist, and it would open Cambodia, India and Nepal at once, which between them cover Phnom Penh, Kathmandu and a set of Indian cities that hold one or two rows each.

gaps.country: several (Latvia, Croatia, Poland, Serbia, Sweden, Taiwan, Ireland, Singapore)
gaps.found: NOT A SOURCE GAP, A READER GAP, AND IT IS CLOSED. About twenty-five verified sources are in a third arrangement nothing here could read: labelled entries running on with no blank line between them, because in HTML the paragraphs separate the entries and the flattened text does not. An entry is a name, an address, then Tel.:, E-Mail:, Sprache:. parse_diplo_block_list.cjs knows this structure exactly and could not see it, because what marks an entry for it is a blank line. scripts/parse_diplo_bold_run.cjs reads it now.
gaps.why:
Kept because the first attempt failed and the reason is worth having. Reading the boundary out of the TEXT, by taking "the next unlabelled line after a labelled one begins the next entry", reads Zagreb well and misreads everything else: a second office address sits under the first telephone number and looks exactly like the next firm, so it published a lawyer called "Billrothstrasse 86". Riga writes "Tel. fuer Notfaelle:", a label with words inside it, so that line became a name and every entry after it was one field out. That reader was written and thrown away.

The boundary is not in the text at all. It is in the markup, and the ministry CMS is consistent: an entry name is a paragraph opening with <strong>, and a section heading is the same thing underlined. Zagreb then reads as 21 firms with 19 stating their own languages, Stockholm as 11 of 11, Taipei as 7 of 7.
gaps.wouldChange: Nothing is outstanding for this shape. Two neighbours of it turned out to be different again and are read elsewhere: Warsaw and Krakow use the ministry address-list markup, where the label is an h4 and the value the div under it, which parse_stacked_labels.cjs reads; Belgrade footnotes its languages as "M = Deutsch, Englisch, S = Deutsch" and so states none per entry, and Dublin states none either. Both are roster sources and depend on the roster claim rather than on a reader.
